rg beats ast-grep 87% of the time. Here's the 13% where it silently fails.

I ran both tools across four production codebases and measured hit rate, precision, and F1. The numbers are not what the ast-grep evangelists suggest.

The standard advice in AI coding tooling is to replace grep with ast-grep. Semantic search, syntax-aware, structured results. The pitch is compelling. The benchmarks tell a more complicated story.

I ran both tools against four production codebases in my Claude Code harness — two Java services and two TypeScript/React codebases — and measured hit rate and F1 across the actual query workload my agents produce. Here's what I found.

Hit rate: rg wins everywhere

Reporg hit rateast-grep hit rateWinner
Java service A (Spring Boot)35.0%8.3%rg
Java service B (Quarkus)38.2%11.6%rg
TypeScript service41.5%28.4%rg
React / TSX frontend40.0%31.7%rg

Hit rate measures whether the tool returns any results at all for a given query. rg wins every repo, by margins ranging from 2.6× on the Java services to 1.26× on the React frontend. For the majority of queries an agent issues — "find usages of X", "find all calls to Y", "where is Z configured" — rg just works and ast-grep does not.

F1: ast-grep wins on dynamic-language repos

Reporg F1ast-grep F1Winner
Java service A (Spring Boot)0.4410.389rg
Java service B (Quarkus)0.4180.371rg
TypeScript service0.2060.473ast-grep
React / TSX frontend0.2160.492ast-grep

F1 measures whether what the tool returns is actually useful — precision and recall combined. ast-grep wins on the TypeScript repos. When it does find something, the result is more precise. rg on dynamic-language code returns more noise: comment matches, string literal matches, partial token matches. The signal-to-noise ratio is worse.

But F1 only applies to queries that returned results. For the queries where ast-grep returned zero — the majority — F1 is undefined. You cannot measure precision on an empty result set.

The 13%: structural pattern queries

Query classrg hit rateast-grep hit raten
Token / identifier lookup71.2%18.4%98
Call site / usage58.3%24.1%54
Config / annotation44.6%19.7%30
Structural pattern0%66.7%27

27 of 209 queries — about 13% — fall into the structural pattern class. These are queries that ask about shape: "find all classes implementing this interface", "find all components with this prop structure", "find all methods matching this call signature." rg returns zero results on every one of them. Not an error. Zero results.

This is the problem. rg does not fail noisily on structural queries. It returns an empty result set, which is indistinguishable from "there are no matches in this codebase." An agent that receives zero results from rg cannot know whether the codebase genuinely has no matches or whether it asked the wrong tool. It will proceed on a false premise.

The concrete case: finding implementors of an interface

Here is the query that surfaced this clearly. I needed to find every class implementing a core domain interface in a Java Spring Boot service with ~350 domain classes. rg query:

rg "implements DomainEntity"

Result: 3 matches. All three were false positives — comment lines and a test fixture. Zero actual implementing classes found.

The reason is that Java class declarations rarely say implements DomainEntity on a single token-searchable line. They say implements DomainEntity, Serializable, or the implements clause spans the line break. rg does not cross line boundaries by default, and multiline patterns are awkward enough that agents rarely write them correctly.

The ast-grep rule:

language: java
rule:
  kind: class_declaration
  has:
    kind: super_interfaces
    stopBy: end
    has:
      kind: type_list
      stopBy: end
      has:
        kind: type_identifier
        stopBy: end
        regex: "^DomainEntity$"

Result: 10 classes. All correct direct implementors across the domain model.

Two things are worth noting. First: the rule required dumping the CST before writing it. dump_syntax_tree(format: cst) on a minimal class declaration reveals the hidden type_list wrapper node — an intermediate node between super_interfaces and type_identifier that is not visible from reading Java syntax. Without knowing it exists, every has check above it fails silently because the target is nested deeper than expected.

Second: stopBy: end is mandatory on every has level above the target. A has without it only checks direct children. The target type identifier lives two levels deep. Without stopBy: end at both levels above it, the rule returns zero — the same silent failure mode as rg, after you invested the time writing a YAML rule.

This is not a beginner mistake. It is what happens when you write ast-grep rules without dumping the CST first. The tool does not warn you. It returns zero.

A second silent failure: wrong language flag

The React frontend in this benchmark is 98% .js and .jsx files, not .tsx. This matters because ast-grep's language flag is exact — specifying language: tsx on a .jsx codebase produces mass-zero results. No parse errors, no warnings. Zero hits.

The correct flag is language: jsx. Specifying tsx on a JSX-only codebase is documented in the benchmark as one of three silent-failure cases that look identical to "no matches found." Always verify the file extension distribution before writing a rule.

This also reveals something about the React frontend codebase itself: it has zero class-based components. The "find all components extending a base class" query returns zero results not because of a tool failure, but because the codebase is fully functional React. The structural query that applies here is shared hook usage — call_expression with a specific hook identifier — which ast-grep handles correctly with language: jsx.

MCP vs CLI for ast-grep rules

One practical note: when running ast-grep from an agent via MCP vs the Bash CLI, the error semantics differ. The Bash CLI returns rc=1 for both parse errors and zero matches — an agent cannot distinguish between "rule was malformed" and "rule was correct but found nothing." The MCP interface returns structured errors that distinguish the two cases. For structural pattern queries where you need to know whether zero results means "not found" or "rule failed," the MCP tool is more reliable than shelling out.

The token cost crossover: the MCP tool list loads once per session at roughly 1.5–2K tokens. For sessions with more than ~10 ast-grep searches the MCP approach is cheaper than loading the Bash CLI overhead per call. For one-off searches, Bash is fine.

The right model: route by query class

The benchmark does not say "use rg" or "use ast-grep." It says the two tools have non-overlapping failure modes, and a correct search layer uses all three with explicit routing:

  • Token / identifier / call-site queries — rg. Fast, high hit rate, low friction. The agent writes a regex and gets results immediately.
  • Structural pattern queries — ast-grep, but only after dumping the CST and verifying the language flag. Never write a rule from the syntax docs alone.
  • Semantic / inheritance resolution — LSP goToImplementation. ast-grep only finds direct implementors; LSP follows what the compiler follows. One caveat: LSP with a persistent cache (like jdtls for Java) is viable from agent flow once warm. LSP without persistent cache (common for TypeScript) is cold on every session — too slow to use inline; use ast-grep instead.

In my harness, this routing is enforced at the skill layer. The search skill classifies the query before dispatching — structural patterns go to ast-grep with a mandatory CST dump step, everything else goes to rg first with ast-grep as a fallback if rg returns zero on a query class where that would be surprising.

The honest summary

rg beats ast-grep on hit rate across every codebase I tested. For the large majority of queries an agent issues in practice, rg returns results and ast-grep does not. On the narrow structural pattern query class — about 13% of workload — ast-grep wins decisively, and rg's zero-result failure is silent and dangerous.

The instinct to "switch to ast-grep" is wrong. The correct instinct is to route by query class, dump the CST before writing any ast-grep rule, verify the language flag matches the actual file extensions in the repo, and treat a zero result from either tool as a reason to check the tool choice before concluding the codebase has no matches.

The search routing logic and CST dump workflow are part of the Claude Code Harness. The full benchmark data and query classification methodology are available on request.
